To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

social ties are important for mammalian survival and thus threats to social connection activate neural regions that are involved in processing basic survival threats and consequently trigger physiological responses that have negative effects on health.

social ties have health implications because social threats and social support are processed by some neural systems that are also involved in the processing of basic threats and safety and that trigger and inhibit, respectively, health-relevant physiological responses.

(1) the health consequences of threats to social connections are mediated, at least in part, by the same physiological responses that are triggered by threats to survival and (2) social support is processed in the same way as safety from basic threats, and inhibits these health-relevant threat responses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the mechanisms by which the social context can shape the body’s physiology and, ultimately, its health.
the question of why social relationships matter for health.
understanding why social relationships are so important for health and well-being and why the absence or loss of social relationships can be so damaging to health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

social ties and health are linked because social ties are a fundamental component of the human experience, and the brain has evolved to process social ties in a manner that has profound health implications.
social ties are important because social ties matter.
the social brain and body are inextricably connected.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social ties are important because of the role that they play in our survival and that they influence the health of the mind and body because of the way that they are processed in the brain.
social connections are a basic biological need and the absence of these connections is a threat to the human organism.

the health effects of social ties and social support are due to their influence on the brain’s processing of threats and safety, and that these processes are mediated by the same neural systems that evolved to protect us against basic threats.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social connections are not just nice-to-haves, but rather that they are critical for our survival and that our bodies treat them as such.
social connections are critical for health and well-being and that the brain processes these connections in a manner similar to how it processes basic threats and safety.
social ties and social support are not just important for health because of their instrumental value, but because they are inherently rewarding and soothing.
